articles.title: ‘India national team is not Indian cricket’: Sunil Gavaskar’s strong message to BCCI and ICC
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sunil Gavaskar has sounded a warning over the relentless demands being placed on Indian cricketers, calling for a rethink of the packed international .
articles.body: Sunil Gavaskar has sounded a warning over the relentless demands being placed on Indian cricketers, calling for a rethink of the packed international calendar and greater emphasis on the domestic game.The former India captain has cautioned against sending players from one series or tournament to another without giving them adequate time to recover. His comments, made in his Sportstar column, come amid growing concerns over the workload on India's players and a recent spate of injuries.A week ago, BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia had attributed the injury problems affecting Indian cricket to the team's heavy match schedule. The board is now keen to find a solution to the issue.With the ICC preparing to discuss the next four-year international calendar cycle beginning in 2027, Gavaskar believes the strain on players needs to be considered while the schedule is being framed.Gavaskar’s warning over player workloadGavaskar referred to the recent meeting held to take stock of Indian cricket and hoped the concerns surrounding the workload would also be reflected in discussions at the ICC.“The recent meeting to take stock of Indian cricket did try to come to grips with the issue. Hopefully, when the ICC meeting to discuss the international cricket calendar over the next cycle of four years from 2027 takes place, the decision-makers will realise that Indian cricketers are neither machines nor sugarcane to be endlessly squeezed for every drop of the juice,” Gavaskar wrote in his column.The former batter's comments come at a time when India's leading players are required to navigate a packed schedule across formats and competitions, increasing the physical demands on an already stretched group.‘The India cricket team is not Indian cricket’Gavaskar also believes the conversation around Indian cricket needs to extend beyond the senior national team.While India's international side remains the most visible part of the sport in the country, he argued that it is ultimately produced by a much wider domestic ecosystem and should not be viewed as synonymous with Indian cricket itself.“The India cricket team is not Indian cricket,” he wrote. “The India cricket team is the by-product of Indian cricket.”For Gavaskar, that distinction is particularly relevant when discussions turn to India's much-praised bench strength.Gavaskar questions India’s three-team depthIndia's ability to field several sides with international experience has often been cited as evidence of the country's enormous talent pool. Gavaskar, however, believes that having enough players to assemble multiple teams does not necessarily mean the domestic system is consistently producing world-class cricketers.He pointed to recent results as a reason to look beyond the perception of India's extraordinary depth and focus instead on strengthening the system that feeds the national team.“The argument that India’s bench strength is such that it can field three teams is good to make claims for the world, but the reality, as recent results have shown, is that one India team is at the moment not good enough to win much silverware. Yes, a gold in the Asian Games will once again rejuvenate the team and give it the confidence for oncoming battles, but unless domestic cricket is prioritised, the pipeline will not produce world beaters. All the best to both our boys and girls to win the gold,” Gavaskar wrote.Gavaskar's argument, therefore, goes beyond simply reducing the workload of India's established stars. He believes the long-term health of Indian cricket depends equally on ensuring that domestic cricket remains strong enough to continually produce players capable of succeeding at the highest level.As the ICC prepares to map out the international calendar from 2027 onwards, Gavaskar's comments put two connected issues under the spotlight: how much cricket India's players are being asked to play and whether the domestic structure is strong enough to sustain the national team in the years ahead.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jasprit Bumrah fit, Harshit Rana out: BCCI fires physio ahead of Afghanistan T20Is
articles.summary: Cricket News: NEW DELHI: The T20I team had its first practice session at the Ferozeshah Kotla on Thursday afternoon ahead of the three-match series against Afghanis.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The T20I team had its first practice session at the Ferozeshah Kotla on Thursday afternoon ahead of the three-match series against Afghanistan starting on Sunday.After months of rehab at the Centre of Excellence (CoE), Jasprit Bumrah and Nitish Kumar Reddy were declared fit to join the team which will fly to Japan for the Asian Games two days after the series.Also on Thursday morning, the Indian cricket board (BCCI) announced that Harshit Rana had suffered another injury during his match simulation test at the CoE on Tuesday. Pacer Yash Thakur was named as his replacement.The recurring injuries have become a roadblock for the team management and selection committee as they try to firm up the preparation for next year’s ODI World Cup in southern Africa.It has emerged that the Indian cricket board (BCCI) has decided to let go of Team India physio Kamlesh Jain in the wake of frequent injuries. TOI had reported on Aug 6 that BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia had pulled up Jain for the spate of injuries to top players.The depth in Indian cricket allows India to make multiple T20I teams. It’s the ODI format that has become a headache for the team management.There has been some disagreement in BCCI circles about sending a full-strength T20I team for the Asiad while there are ODIs lined up against West Indies.Even as Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson went through their batting sessions in the practice area, head coach Gautam Gambhir was seen spending more time with T20I captain Shreyas Iyer and Washington Sundar — two integral members of the ODI team — when they were batting at the centre square.When the ODI series against West Indies starts in Thiruvananthapuram on Sept 27, Gambhir will be without first-choice ODI players like Bumrah, Iyer, Washington, Axar Patel, Ishan Kishan and Reddy.There’s no clarity about when allrounder Hardik Pandya will be available even as he undergoes an unending rehab at the CoE.While the World Cup may seem a year away, the number of ODIs are few and far between. It has left very little breathing space for the team management and the selectors to firm up the ODI core team.Meanwhile, India’s fast bowling coach Morne Morkel hasn’t yet joined the team. Sources said he is yet to receive his visa renewal.First T20I to go ahead despite traffic police request to rescheduleThe Delhi and District Cricket Association (DDCA) said that the first T20I on Sept 13 will go ahead as scheduled even as the Delhi traffic police wrote a letter to the association requesting to move the match in light of the BRICS summit.In a letter, the DCP (traffic) said the summit would require extensive traffic arrangements, including VVIP/VIP route regulation and deployment of personnel.However, DDCA later posted on X saying the match was on.“The 1st T20I will go ahead as scheduled. Following a meeting with Delhi traffic police, DDCA has been assured of all support,” the association said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 49ers TE injury vs. Rams ‘wasn’t good’ per Kyle Shanahan
articles.summary: The San Francisco 49ers beat the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 on Thursday night, but they may have lost a tight end for a while.
articles.body:
The San Francisco 49ers beat the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 at Melbourne Cricket Ground on Thursday night to improve to 1-0 on the season, but during the game, they lost a key player who caught five touchdowns last year.

In the second quarter, 49ers tight end Jake Tonges suffered a knee injury, and trainers had to cart him back to the locker room. While he was questionable to return, he didn't play another snap in the victory.

After the game, 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan didn't have the best injury update.

"It wasn't good," Shanahan said. "It's not ACL. It's MCL, I believe. But there are some issues with it that we gotta see how it is. There's a little more information to it, but we don't know yet."

With George Kittle easing back into action after returning quickly from a torn Achilles, the 49ers might have to rely on him more going forward. They also have Luke Farrell on the 53-man roster and both Brayden Willis and Khalil Dinkins on the practice squad at the position.

articles.title: ‘He is not being neglected’: Sourav Ganguly’s blunt verdict on Mohammed Shami
articles.summary: Cricket News: Sourav Ganguly has rejected the suggestion that Mohammed Shami is being overlooked by India's selectors, saying the veteran pacer has already achieved.
articles.body: Sourav Ganguly has rejected the suggestion that Mohammed Shami is being overlooked by India's selectors, saying the veteran pacer has already achieved plenty and remains “an absolute champion”.Shami has not played for India since the Champions Trophy 2025, where he was an important part of the side that won the title. The 36-year-old has continued to feature in domestic cricket during his absence from the national team and on Thursday helped East Zone end a 13-year wait for the Duleep Trophy.Ganguly, speaking to reporters at the Eden Gardens, said Shami's continued commitment to domestic cricket and his performances were particularly encouraging.“What makes me happy for Shami is that he turns out day in and day out in domestic cricket and performs. It is terrific to see. He has achieved so much," Ganguly said.With Shami still producing performances in domestic cricket, Ganguly was asked whether the pacer could force his way back into India's plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup.The former India captain, however, felt it was far too early to make such a prediction, pointing out that the tournament is still some distance away.“That's a long way. I can't comment. It's in October (next year). It's a long way," he said.Ganguly was also asked whether he believed Shami was being neglected by the senior men's selection panel.He strongly disagreed, while acknowledging that being left out can become part of a cricketer's career as age advances. Ganguly drew on his own experience of being dropped from India's World Cup plans despite having already crossed the 10,000-run mark in international cricket.“He is not being neglected. He has played a lot. He is an absolute champion. But as you grow older, this happens. When I got left out from World Cup one-day cricket for a year, after scoring 10,000 runs, I found my way to come back. So this happens with everyone.”The comments came on a day when Ganguly also congratulated East Zone on their Duleep Trophy triumph, which ended a long wait for the title.Ganguly backs Ishan Kishan for Test returnGanguly also had words of praise for East Zone captain Ishan Kishan, whose performances in the Duleep Trophy have strengthened his case for a possible return to India's Test side.The CAB president revealed that he had spoken to Kishan on Thursday and backed the wicketkeeper-batter to keep targeting Test cricket.“I spoke to Kishan this afternoon. It's terrific and remarkable. Every young player wants to play Test cricket, and hopefully he will. He played exceptionally well in all the finals of the Vijay Hazare, Syed Mushtaq Ali, and Duleep Trophy.”Ganguly stressed the importance of Test cricket for young players and highlighted Kishan's ability to produce runs when the stakes are highest.“If he performs, I think for every young player Test cricket should be important. They must want to play Test cricket and hopefully he will. He gets runs in big matches.... Vijay Hazare final, Mushtaq final, Duleep Trophy final.”Kishan's last Test appearance for India came against the West Indies in July 2023. Since then, he has been working his way back into contention, and his latest run of performances has given his Test ambitions another boost.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'He made us all believe': How Dhoni is quietly shaping Jharkhand's next generation
articles.summary: Cricket News: KOLKATA: Mahendra Singh Dhoni’s influence on Jharkhand cricket has never needed an official designation. Even after stepping away from the domestic cr.
articles.body: KOLKATA: Mahendra Singh Dhoni’s influence on Jharkhand cricket has never needed an official designation. Even after stepping away from the domestic cricket long ago, the former India captain continues to leave his imprint quietly, helping shape a young generation that is now beginning to make its presence felt at the highest domestic level across formats.East Zone’s Duleep Trophy triumph on Thursday, their first since 2012, offered perhaps the clearest indication yet of the strength of Jharkhand’s emerging batting core. Captain Ishan Kishan led from the front, aggregating 350 runs in the final, while Shikhar Mohan, Kumar Kushagra, Md Kounain Quraishi and Anukul Roy were among the Jharkhand players who made significant contributions during the campaign.The title, naturally, was a collective East Zone achievement. Bengal supplied considerable experience through Mohammed Shami, Mukesh Kumar, Abhimanyu Easwaran, Sudip Gharami and Shahbaz Ahmed, while Bihar’s teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi also made his mark in the semifinal with the fastest half-century in the history of the tournament. But the performance of Jharkhand’s young middle-order batters provided one of the strongest threads running through East Zone’s campaign.And behind that progression, there is a familiar figure who continues to offer guidance without occupying any formal role.“Whenever he is free and in Ranchi, he visits the (JSCA) stadium. From juniors to seniors, when camps are going on, he comes himself, talks to people and gets involved. When we won Mushtaq Ali last year, the first congratulatory message I received was by Mahi bhai,” JSCA secretary and former India and Jharkhand batter Saurabh Tiwary said of Dhoni.“He keeps telling us which players are good and should be watched. He also speaks to players whenever they get an opportunity to meet him and tells them how to perform. The most important thing he discusses with them is how to read the game. That is a huge mental factor when you are playing at the top level,” Tiwary told TOI on Thursday.Once a regular in the Indian Premier League, Tiwary said Dhoni’s involvement has grown significantly and that his interest in the state setup remains remarkably close. Dhoni can, according to Tiwary, “name Jharkhand’s playing XI any day and keeps a close watch on emerging players”.That influence is not necessarily about technical instruction. It is about understanding what it takes to survive and succeed at the top level — something Dhoni knows better than most.Former Jharkhand player Ishank Jaggi and now their U-23 coach, who has also worked closely with several of the state’s younger cricketers, believes the current crop has developed a greater understanding of their game.“MSD was the first guy playing for the country from Jharkhand. He made us all believe that players from Jharkhand can also be at the top level,” Jaggi said.According to Jaggi, the Player of the Match in the 2012 Duleep Trophy final – the last time East Zone was triumphant – Dhoni remains closely connected with the state’s cricket ecosystem despite his busy schedule.“Whenever he is in Ranchi and free, he makes sure he is at the (JSCA) stadium. Coaches and players ask him about different situations and he shares his experiences. Whether it’s the men’s team or the women’s team, everybody benefits from his inputs.”Jaggi also believes the likes of Kushagra and Mohan are capable of pushing for India selection. Shikhar, in particular, has emerged as one of Jharkhand’s most promising all-round young cricketers, with his batting, bowling and fielding across formats drawing praise from Tiwary.“I think in the coming three years you will see even more good players coming through,” Tiwary said. “The future looks very good for Jharkhand.”That optimism is rooted in more than one successful Duleep Trophy campaign and their maiden Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy triumph last year under Kishan and with same set-up. Tiwary pointed to a growing system in which former players are now involved in coaching, selection and administration, bringing with them a close understanding of the players and the pathway they have travelled.For a generation that grew up idolising Dhoni, he remains the most influential link between Jharkhand’s cricketing past and its future and East Zone’s Duleep Trophy triumph offered a glimpse of what may lie ahead. The likes of Kishan, Kushagra, Shikhar, Roy and Quraishi are already making their mark beyond state cricket as Jharkhand’s former players continue to mentor the next batch, backed by Dhoni’s quiet but enduring guidance.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Embarrassing': Wasim Akram slams Pakistan's shocking mid-tour changes
articles.summary: Cricket News: Former Pakistan captain Wasim Akram has criticised the major changes made to the team in the middle of its England tour, calling the situation “embarr.
articles.body: Former Pakistan captain Wasim Akram has criticised the major changes made to the team in the middle of its England tour, calling the situation “embarrassing” and pointing to a lack of communication within the setup.Akram said Pakistan need more consistency and better communication if they want to improve their performances.“Consistency is the key, of course, but for how long? When seven players and two coaches return in the middle of a tour, it is embarrassing for the team and the captain, and it also shows there is a lack of communication,” Akram said while speaking to YouTuber Furqan Bhatti.Akram believes Pakistan still have enough talent to compete at the highest level. He said his experience with Pakistan Super League (PSL) teams has given him a close look at the country’s players.“I have been involved in the PSL with these teams for the past four to five years, so I have seen the situation closely. In my view, the talent is there. Coaches may change, but the core players remain largely the same,” he said.‘Give the system four to five years’The former Pakistan captain also asked the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) to give the domestic system enough time to produce results instead of making regular changes.“Everyone has to give the system at least three to four years. Whoever comes in next should avoid constantly changing the first-class structure. Give it four to five years, and then you will see the results,” he said.Akram also stressed the need to strengthen cricket at the grassroots level. He called for greater focus on club, school and college cricket to ensure a steady supply of talent.“We need to revive club cricket as well as school and college cricket. If grassroots cricket disappears, where will the talent come from? The PCB only takes players after they reach a certain stage,” Akram added.Robinson puts Pakistan in deep troubleMeanwhile, Pakistan’s problems on the England tour continued at Edgbaston as Ollie Robinson struck twice in his opening over on Thursday.Robinson, man of the match in the first two Tests, took a wicket with the first ball of Pakistan’s second innings and struck again three deliveries later.Pakistan reached 52-2 before rain brought an early end to play on day two. They still needed 268 runs to make England bat again.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘My rhythm wasn't quite there’: Mohammed Siraj reveals what went wrong in Sri Lanka
articles.summary: Cricket News: Mohammed Siraj believes a two-month break from competitive cricket was behind the loss of pace and rhythm that affected him during India's recent Test.
articles.body: Mohammed Siraj believes a two-month break from competitive cricket was behind the loss of pace and rhythm that affected him during India's recent Test tour of Sri Lanka.The India pacer, however, feels his stint in the Duleep Trophy has helped him rediscover the rhythm he needs before another international season gets underway.Siraj bowled 41 overs for South Zone in the Duleep Trophy final against East Zone at Chepauk, and despite a difficult outing in the first innings, he believes the workload was exactly what his body needed after the lengthy break.During the two-Test series in Sri Lanka, Siraj's pace was noticeably down. Instead of operating in his usual early-to-mid 140s, he was bowling in the late 120s. Across the four innings, he sent down 44 overs but was unable to trouble the Sri Lankan batters consistently, with the spinners naturally taking on the bulk of the workload.‘My rhythm wasn't quite there’Siraj said the problem began with the abrupt transition from a long break into international cricket."Coming off a two-month break straight into a match, my rhythm wasn't quite there. I'm purely a rhythm bowler. If I'm not in sync, I simply can't explode through the crease," Siraj told media after the Duleep Trophy final here.The pacer explained that the disruption was particularly evident in his run-up, which affected the momentum he relies on to generate pace."That was the struggle in Sri Lanka—my run-up felt disjointed. Some strides were too short, others were too long, and that broke my flow and cost me pace," he added.Siraj's two-month break came after the one-off Test against Afghanistan, which ended on June 8. He then returned to action on India's tour of Sri Lanka, which began with a game against SLC XI on August 7.Long spells help Siraj find his rhythm againThe Duleep Trophy final offered Siraj the chance to put in the kind of workload he felt was necessary to get his body functioning naturally again."Out here, everything clicked into place, and the pace followed naturally. Yes, it was very tough. We came straight from Sri Lanka, where we spent three and a half days fielding in the second Test (at Colombo), and within a week, we were out here playing in Chennai's sweltering heat."But for me, it comes down to passion. When you're representing your country, you can’t make excuses. You have to give every ounce of effort for your team and nation.”Siraj endured a tough first innings, as East Zone's batters attacked him for 140 runs from his 25 overs. He had to wait until the second innings to claim a wicket.But the figures did not concern him as much as getting through a substantial workload.“Even if I didn't get the wickets to show for it today, that hard work will pay off at the international level.”Rhythm, not wickets, was Siraj’s prioritySiraj made it clear that his primary objective in playing the Duleep Trophy was not to inflate his First Class wicket tally. Instead, he wanted to regain the fluency in his bowling that had deserted him after the two-month layoff.“Heading into this game, finding that flow was my primary goal. Playing this match helped me tremendously. After two months off, your body doesn't react the same way—everything feels a beat slower. Getting through this game got my body moving again and brought my rhythm right back,” he said.The 32-year-old said his body is better suited to sustained workloads than extended periods away from cricket. While the break gave him an opportunity to work on other aspects, including fitness parameters, it also left him feeling sluggish when he returned to bowling."That's just how my body works. My body doesn't handle long breaks well. A short breather is fine, but in my 10-year career, I had never taken two full months off. So, the more overs I bowl, the better I get."If I don't bowl extended spells, my rhythm won't return. The break left my body feeling sluggish at the crease. I bowled spells of 10 and 11 overs, and that's exactly what locked me back into rhythm,” he noted.The lack of rhythm had also created the impression that Siraj was operating with a shorter run-up. He explained that the issue was not a deliberate change to his approach, but simply his body adjusting after the extended break."My approach (to bowling crease) relies on fluid, uninterrupted acceleration rather than staccato steps. Coming back after a two-month layoff, my body was just recalibrating its stride lengths. In this match, it all felt completely natural again.“I told myself to forget the outcome and just run in with a good, natural rhythm. The moment I did that, the old Siraj was back in action, and the ball started coming out beautifully,” he said.Shami’s advice helped SirajSiraj also had the opportunity to spend time with former India teammate Mohammed Shami, who represented East Zone in the Duleep Trophy final.Siraj described their interaction as a casual chat, but Shami revealed that he had offered his former bowling partner some advice after noticing that Siraj was struggling to find his natural rhythm in the first innings.“Whenever I interact with guys I’ve played with or share a good bond with, I focus on their skill. In the first innings, Siraj wasn’t quite finding his natural rhythm.“I just reminded him that to get back on top, he needed to return to his core strengths. When your run-up and rhythm are in sync, your line and length fall into place automatically,” said Shami.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'He shouldn't be here': Nasser Hussain bashes Pakistan with Virender Sehwag example
articles.summary: Cricket News: Former England captain Nasser Hussain has slammed Pakistan’s decision to bring Saim Ayub into the Test team straight from the Caribbean Premier League.
articles.body: Former England captain Nasser Hussain has slammed Pakistan’s decision to bring Saim Ayub into the Test team straight from the Caribbean Premier League (CPL), saying the young batter “shouldn't be here”.Ayub’s return to the Pakistan Test team ended in a nightmare as he was dismissed for a duck in both innings of the third Test against England at Edgbaston. The young opener faced only 11 balls across the two innings, with England pacer Ollie Robinson dismissing him on both occasions.Ayub had arrived in England after playing T20 cricket in the CPL. Hussain questioned why Pakistan chose to bring him into a Test match without enough preparation for the conditions.Speaking on Sky Sports after Pakistan finished Day 2 at 52-2 in their second innings, Hussain said Ayub should not have been picked for the Test.“The truth is he shouldn't be here. He came from the CPL and hasn't played first-class cricket in some time,” Hussain said during a post-day show on Sky Sports.Hussain said bringing a player directly from T20 cricket into a Test in England was a poor decision.“I don't know who thinks it's the right thing to fly someone over from foreign conditions, playing a completely different format, and think they're going to be fine in these conditions against a Dukes ball, against Ollie Robinson and England's bowling attack,” Hussain asserted, explaining why Ayub was destined to fail in these conditions against a team of the calibre of England.Hussain recalls Sehwag exampleHussain also recalled what happened when India once took a similar approach with Virender Sehwag.Sehwag was flown into England without enough match practice and struggled at the same ground. Hussain said that if even a player of Sehwag’s experience could struggle, Pakistan should not have expected Ayub to immediately succeed.“Virender Sehwag tried it on this ground, if you remember... they flew him in. Virender Sehwag got a pair, and that's Virender Sehwag, who's a better, more experienced player than Saim,” highlighted Hussain.Hussain said Ayub must take some responsibility for the shot he played, but he questioned the decision-makers who selected him.“So a bit of responsibility goes to the lad for the shot he played. But also, whoever thought that was a seriously good decision and that he was going to go okay this week?”“It is just a sort of disrespect and disregard for Test match cricket. Test match cricket, as any cricketer will tell you, is the toughest format. Batting at the top of the order in England is the toughest task, and you just feel you can fly someone in from some part of the world and go, Good luck,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘My name was not even in the FIR’: How a former India cricketer's 22-year ordeal ended in acquittal after a controversial UK tour, arrest and Tihar Jail
articles.summary: Cricket News: For most cricketers, the innings that define them are played out in the middle. Jacob Martin's longest battle was fought in a courtroom.The former Ind.
articles.body: For most cricketers, the innings that define them are played out in the middle. Jacob Martin's longest battle was fought in a courtroom.The former India batsman was acquitted in a 22-year-old criminal case tied to a controversial 2004 cricket tour of the United Kingdom. The Patiala House Court in Delhi cleared the Vadodara resident of all charges: forgery, cheating, criminal conspiracy and offences under the Passport Act.The case traced back to a 2004 FIR invoking Sections 420, 468, 471 and 120B of the IPC alongside Section 12 of the Passport Act. Prosecutors alleged a forged UK immigration stamp, dubious travel arrangements and financial transactions involving Martin. None of it held up.Nor did the court find credible evidence of Martin owning or controlling Ajwa Sports Club, the club at the centre of the allegations. Witness after witness failed to back the prosecution's case, and the charges collapsed.Martin is 54 now. The verdict closes a chapter that ran for more than two decades and reshaped both his career and his life outside it.From Ranji runs to the India capBefore any of this, Martin had built a name as one of domestic cricket's most reliable middle-order batsmen. Born in Baroda, he made his living on concentration and the sheer willingness to bat time. His breakout came in the 1998-99 Ranji Trophy, when he crossed 1,000 runs for the season and became only the sixth batter in the competition's history to do so.That run brought him national attention, and eventually a India call-up.His first-class career dwarfs his international one. Martin played 138 first-class matches, scored over 9,000 runs, hit 23 centuries and averaged above 46. He also captained Baroda to the 2000-01 Ranji Trophy, still the team's most recent title, and later returned to Baroda cricket as a coach.At the international level, though, it never really took off. Ten ODIs, a debut against the West Indies in Toronto in 1999, and a stretch between 1999 and 2001 in which he managed 158 runs at 22.57.The tour that changed everythingThe number that shadows Martin's career isn't 10 caps or 9,000 first-class runs. It's 22, the years the case hung over him.By his account, it started with a team associated with him that travelled to the UK in 2004. Most of the players came home. One didn't, overstaying his six-month visa. That player, Martin says, arranged a fake immigration stamp through a contact in Britain. He was eventually deported and picked up at Indira Gandhi International Airport for questioning.Martin insists his name wasn't in the original FIR at all, that he was pulled into the investigation later, partly because of who he was."In 2004 a team of mine had gone, which had gone to the UK to play. That team which went to play in England in 2004, everyone came back except one boy who stayed back in the UK. Because the visa had a validity of 6 months, he could stay for 6 months, but he overstayed for more than 6 months, so what happened was that he got fake stamping done there through someone. After getting fake stamping done, when he came back to India, he was deported from the UK, so he was caught at the IGI airport, and then he was questioned," Martin said.Police told a different story. They alleged Martin and an associate had arranged the boy's trip under the pretence of a cricket tour, with money involved, and that Ajwa Sports Club, described as a bogus outfit, was used in the arrangement. There was even a suggestion of human trafficking or an illegal-immigration racket.None of it stood up in court.Arrest, Tihar and a career quietly dismantledMartin was arrested in Delhi and spent time in Tihar Jail while the case crawled through the system.It still hadn't been resolved by 2016, when the Baroda Cricket Association named him Ranji Trophy coach, a decision that drew criticism given that the case was still pending.Away from the field, the damage was more direct. Martin says he lost his job with the Railways over the case and could never get a foothold with the BCCI. Two decades of uncertainty took their toll."My name was not even in the FIR, but when the investigation took place, I was involved in this case because the name was big and I was an international cricketer, because of that. And after the case ended, this... now, after 22 years... during these 22 years, I was not getting any answers from the BCCI either; I lost my job in the railways. So I had a lot of stress because of this, but this judgment that has come now- I have got a clean chit; it will be a big settlement for my life and very... after 22 years, this... appeal I have received is a very big U-turn for my life," he added.The court case wasn't the only thing testing him. In December 2018, Martin was badly injured in a road accident in Vadodara, with his lung and liver both damaged. He was put on a ventilator, spent nearly a month in intensive care, and for a while his condition was critical.Former teammates and administrators rallied to help cover his treatment.More than two decades after that tour to England, Martin's legal ordeal has ended. It won't undo the years he lost. But it gives him something he hadn't had in a long while: a life after cricket that isn't defined by a case still hanging over him.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'There’s a lot of quality in Pakistan': Team coach defends players despite horror run in England
articles.summary: Cricket News: Pakistan's difficult tour of England has exposed plenty of problems with the bat, but batting coach Michael Smith believes the team's young players ne.
articles.body: Pakistan's difficult tour of England has exposed plenty of problems with the bat, but batting coach Michael Smith believes the team's young players need time and exposure to the Test environment before they can be judged.Pakistan's struggles continued on the second day of the ongoing Test in Birmingham, with the visitors reaching 52/2 in their second innings before persistent rain brought an early end to play. They remained 268 runs behind England.Pakistan's batting has been horrendous, to say the least. They have managed scores of 171, 135, 110, 194 and 133 all out in their five innings so far. They have not once crossed the 200-run mark.With Pakistan already suffering heavy defeats in the first two Tests at Headingley and Lord's, the team has undergone a significant transition during the tour. Seven players, including wicketkeeper Mohammad Rizwan, opening batter Imam-ul-Haq and T20 captain Salman Ali Agha, were sent home midway through the series.Only Babar Azam and Shan Masood among Pakistan's current top seven have previously toured England.Smith urges patience with Pakistan's young battersSmith acknowledged that Pakistan are going through a period of change but insisted there is enough talent coming through to eventually strengthen the side."For me there's a lot of quality in Pakistan. We've seen it for many years and lots of countries go through slight changes. This is one where we've got some younger players with some experienced players but it's the learning and how quickly we can get them to learn and get comfortable in the Test environment to really help them from a long-term point of view," Smith told reporters following the second day’s play.The batting coach admitted that one of Pakistan's biggest shortcomings has been their inability to convert promising starts into long stays at the crease.The visitors have shown flashes of resilience during the series, but those moments have rarely lasted long enough to alter the course of matches."We've shown some real good signs but just not for long enough and I think that's probably the biggest lesson is that we need some of our guys to be playing for hours at times and in certain game plans," Smith said.Smith pointed to Saud Shakeel, Azan Awais and Shan Masood as players who have already demonstrated that they can handle the demands of Test batting, but stressed that Pakistan need them to sustain that level for much longer."I think Saud Shakeel has shown us at times, Azan Awais has shown us and Shan too, but we need that for hours and not just for half a session or so. Some of the players, it's their first tour of England and they haven't got a lot of Test experience so they are learning some challenging lessons along the way and they have to learn on the Test circuit which is a challenging one.," he added.The challenge has been particularly pronounced in England, where several members of the current batting group are experiencing English conditions for the first time.Despite Pakistan's results, Smith said the mood within the camp remained positive and urged people not to make early judgments about the younger members of the squad.He also acknowledged that Pakistan have been up against a strong England bowling attack operating in familiar home conditions.“It’s been tough, it’s been challenging but let’s not take away the fact that we've come up against a really good bowling unit in home conditions who've been excellent,” Smith said.The batting coach believes the more telling assessment of this group will come when Pakistan return to England in the future, provided many of the same players remain part of the side.“I suppose we might not see the sort of success we want to see now but hopefully if a lot of these players are back on our next UK tour we'll really see an upward trend and I think that's the time to really judge them - especially some of the younger players who get their first taste of the English type of conditions," said Smith.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 10 days, 1,981 runs, no winner: In the longest-ever Test, England were 42 runs from victory vs South Africa when a ship to home forced a draw
articles.summary: Cricket News: In an era when a Test match can be over in three or four days, it is almost impossible to imagine a game continuing for 10 days. But in 1939, England .
articles.body: In an era when a Test match can be over in three or four days, it is almost impossible to imagine a game continuing for 10 days. But in 1939, England and South Africa played a Test with no time limit. It lasted 43 hours and 16 minutes, produced 1,981 runs, and still did not have a winner.The reason the match finally ended? England had a ship to catch.When Test matches had no time limitTest cricket has always been about patience. Today, five days is considered the ultimate examination, but there was a time when Test matches were played until there was a winner. The most extraordinary example came in Durban, South Africa, in March 1939. It became known as the “Timeless Test” and remains the longest Test match ever played.England were touring South Africa for a five-Test series. With England leading 1-0 going into the final Test, the teams agreed that the match would be played to a finish, without a fixed time limit. The game began at Kingsmead on 3 March 1939, with South Africa choosing to bat.South Africa bat for nearly three daysOn a pitch that offered little assistance to the bowlers, South Africa batted for almost three days and made 530. Pieter van der Bijl scored 125 and Dudley Nourse made 103, with South Africa's first innings taking around 13 hours of playing time. England replied with 316, giving South Africa a 214-run lead.A 696-run target for EnglandSouth Africa had the option of enforcing the follow-on but chose to bat again. Captain Alan Melville's side added another 481 runs, leaving England with a massive target of 696. England began their fourth innings on 9 March. With no time limit, there was no need to panic. And slowly, the impossible started to look possible.Bill Edrich produced a magnificent 219, while Gerry Gibb scored 120. Then England captain Wally Hammond added 140. England kept batting, kept scoring and kept eating into the enormous target. Eventually, they reached 654/5. They needed just 42 more runs to win. After 10 days of play, England were suddenly on the verge of completing one of the greatest fourth-innings chases in Test history. Then came the rain.The timeless Test finally ran out of timeRain had already interrupted the match several times, but the pitch repeatedly recovered well enough for play to continue. On 14 March, England resumed with victory within reach. Hammond was dismissed for 140 and, with the score at 654/5, rain stopped play again. England needed only 42 runs. But the problem was no longer the weather.It was the calendar. England had a train and a ship to catch England's tour had already been planned around their journey home. The team had to travel from Durban to Cape Town by train, where they were due to board the Athlone Castle for the voyage back to Britain on 17 March.The “Timeless Test” might have had no cricketing deadline, but England's travel arrangements did. There was no realistic way for the match to continue indefinitely. The captains eventually agreed to end the game. England were left stranded at 654/5, just 42 runs short of victory.The match was declared a draw. 10 days, 1,981 runs and no winner The match took place across 12 calendar days, with 10 days of actual play. It remains the longest Test match in men's cricket history, according to Guinness World Records.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
